reading.rtitle: Halfway There -- A Progress Check for International Physicians
paras: TWO DIFFERENT SCORES. Fluency and accuracy are not the same thing. A resident who speaks fast, with many small mistakes, has good fluency but weak accuracy. A resident who speaks slowly and perfectly has the opposite profile. Most international physicians are much stronger in one than in the other, so measure them separately.

THEN AND NOW. Every few months, compare your English with your own benchmark, not with a native speaker. Is a consultation easier than it was six months ago? Is a written case report faster? A ten-minute recording of one case presentation, made at the start and at the halfway point, is the most honest test you can find.

THE BLIND SPOT. Although most physicians know their strengths, few can see their blind spots. Doctors trained in Portuguese, for example, often drop articles or forget the s in the third person, and they rarely notice it. Therefore, ask for feedback, and keep track of the mistakes that come back again and again.

THE NEXT BLOCK. Choose one thing to build on and one thing to brush up on. Physicians practicing for ten consistent minutes a day usually make more progress than physicians studying for five hours on a Sunday. If you can do that, you are on track.

listenings.text: Halfway through the year, I sit down with every international resident for a progress check, and I always measure two things separately. The first is fluency: can you present a patient without long pauses? The second is accuracy: are the words and the grammar correct? Most residents are much stronger in one than in the other. Some are fast and confident, but they make the same small mistakes every day. Others are perfectly correct, but they speak so slowly that the team stops listening. Then I ask two questions. What is easier now than in your first month? And what still makes you nervous? The answers are usually more useful than any test. Although nobody likes to hear about their weaknesses, I always give one honest piece of feedback. And I ask every resident to keep track of their own mistakes, in a list, for two weeks. Residents doing this for two weeks usually find their blind spot without my help.

For a long time, I thought my English was good. I was fast, and people understood me, so I never asked for feedback. Then, halfway through my first year, my program director asked me to record one case presentation. I avoided it for a month. When I finally listened to the recording, I was surprised. My fluency was fine, but I dropped the word the in almost every sentence. Patient has rash on arm. Biopsy was negative. Nobody had ever told me, because everybody understood the message. However, it did not sound professional. So I made a simple plan. I recorded one case presentation a week, and I counted the missing articles. The first week, there were twenty-three. After two months, there were four. It is not perfect yet, but now I know my blind spot, and I am on track.

extra_audio.text: Twenty lessons ago, I was nervous in every consultation in English. Now my listening is much faster, and I can present a case without notes. Although my fluency has improved, accuracy is still my blind spot. Therefore, I keep track of my mistakes in a small notebook. In the next block, I want to brush up on my written English.
